title: Search, Seizure, and Warrants
in30Seconds: The Fourth Amendment does not forbid police from searching. It forbids unreasonable searches and seizures, and it tells you what a warrant must contain. Working with it means answering three questions in order: was this a search or a seizure at all, did officers have a warrant, and if not does a recognized exception cover what they did. This lesson walks that sequence through the cases that built it. Educational material about United States law, not legal advice.
whyItMatters: Almost every criminal case that turns on physical evidence turns first on the Fourth Amendment. Suppression motions decide what a jury will ever hear, which is why the framework shows up in criminal justice surveys, criminal procedure courses, police academy training, and paralegal programs alike. It is also the part of constitutional law that changes fastest, because each new sensing technology forces courts to ask again what privacy the Amendment preserves. Learning the sequence rather than a list of case names is what lets you reason about a fact pattern nobody has litigated yet, including whatever device replaces the one in your pocket.
learningObjectives: Define a Fourth Amendment search using both the Katz reasonable-expectation-of-privacy test and the trespass theory restored in United States v. Jones.
Distinguish a consensual encounter from a seizure of a person under Bostick, Hodari D., and Torres v. Madrid.
Explain what probable cause, oath or affirmation, and particularity each require of a valid warrant.
Apply the recognized warrant exceptions - consent, exigency, search incident to arrest, the automobile exception, plain view, and the Terry frisk - to a described encounter.
Analyze why a search that is lawful under federal doctrine may still be unlawful under a state constitution.

collegeVersion.heading: Two clauses, and the order of the questions
collegeVersion.body:
The Fourth Amendment is one sentence with two working parts. The first secures the right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures. The second says no warrants shall issue but upon probable cause, supported by oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched and the persons or things to be seized. Notice what the text does not say: it never states that police must always get a warrant. It says searching must not be unreasonable, and it says what a warrant must rest on when one is used.

Courts filled that gap with a presumption. Katz v. United States (1967) described searches conducted without prior approval by a judge or magistrate as per se unreasonable, subject only to a few specifically established and well-delineated exceptions - a sentence the Court was still quoting in Arizona v. Gant in 2009. Kentucky v. King (2011) put it plainly: warrantless searches inside a home are presumptively unreasonable, but the presumption can be overcome when the exigencies of a situation make a warrantless search objectively reasonable. The practical law therefore lives in the exceptions, and a student who memorizes the presumption without them has learned the smaller half.

Work any problem in this order. First, did government action amount to a search or a seizure? If not, the Amendment has nothing to say and the analysis stops. Second, was there a warrant, and was it valid? Third, if there was no warrant, does a recognized exception apply? Only after those three does the remedial question - what happens to the evidence - arise. The Amendment constrains government actors, and it reaches state and local police because Mapp v. Ohio (1961) made evidence obtained in violation of it inadmissible in state criminal trials.

collegeVersion.heading: What counts as a search
collegeVersion.body:
For most of the Amendment's history the answer was physical: a search meant a trespass on a protected place. Katz ended that monopoly. FBI agents had taped a listening device to the outside of a public telephone booth, entering nothing, and the government argued that settled it. Justice Stewart's opinion for the Court answered that the Fourth Amendment protects people, not places, so its reach cannot turn on the presence or absence of a physical intrusion. The Court added a limit in the same breath that students often skip: what a person knowingly exposes to the public, even in his own home or office, is not protected.

The test everyone cites is not in the majority opinion. Justice Harlan, concurring, described a twofold requirement - that a person have exhibited an actual, subjective expectation of privacy, and that the expectation be one society is prepared to recognize as reasonable. Later cases adopted that formulation, and it is what courts mean by the Katz test.

The trespass idea never died. In United States v. Jones (2012) agents attached a GPS tracker to a car and monitored it for 28 days, having installed it outside the terms of the warrant they held. Justice Scalia's opinion found a search without reaching privacy at all: the government had physically intruded on a constitutionally enumerated effect in order to obtain information. Katz, the Court said, has been added to, but not substituted for, the common-law trespassory test. Two routes, either sufficient.

Sensing technology gets its own line of cases. Kyllo v. United States (2001) held that pointing a thermal imager at a house was a search, because using a device not in general public use to learn details of a home's interior that would previously have required physical intrusion is exactly what the Amendment preserves against. Carpenter v. United States (2018) reached records rather than rooms: acquiring 127 days of a suspect's historical cell-site location information was a search, and a Stored Communications Act order resting on reasonable grounds was not enough, because that showing falls well short of probable cause. The Court called the decision narrow and left conventional surveillance and case-specific exceptions alone.

collegeVersion.heading: What counts as a seizure of a person
collegeVersion.body:
Property is seized when the government meaningfully interferes with a possessory interest. A person is seized on a different test, and the line matters because officers may talk to anyone without justification at all. United States v. Mendenhall (1980) supplied the phrase: a person has been seized only if, in view of all the circumstances, a reasonable person would have believed he was not free to leave. That passage drew only two votes in Mendenhall itself, but later majorities adopted it. The opinion also listed the tells - several officers present, a displayed weapon, physical touching, or language or tone indicating that compliance is expected.

Florida v. Bostick (1991) fixed a defect in that phrasing. Officers were questioning passengers on a stopped bus, and no passenger wanted to leave a bus they had paid to ride. The Florida Supreme Court had declared every such encounter a seizure. Justice O'Connor's opinion rejected the per se rule and restated the question: whether a reasonable person would feel free to decline the officers' requests or otherwise terminate the encounter.

California v. Hodari D. (1991) added the timing rule. A seizure requires either the application of physical force, however slight, or - absent force - submission to a show of authority. Hodari kept running after an officer gave chase, so he was not seized until he was tackled, and the drugs he threw away while running were not the fruit of any seizure. Torres v. Madrid (2021) then completed the force half: applying physical force to a person's body with intent to restrain is a seizure even if the person does not submit and is not subdued. The inquiry is objective - does the conduct manifest an intent to restrain - not whether the officer succeeded.

collegeVersion.heading: What a valid warrant requires
collegeVersion.body:
A warrant is an ex ante permission slip from someone who is not investigating the case. Three elements make it valid. Probable cause is the quantum of justification, and Illinois v. Gates (1983) defines how it is measured. The Court discarded the rigid two-pronged test that had governed informant tips and adopted a totality-of-the-circumstances approach: the issuing magistrate makes a practical, common-sense decision whether, given everything in the affidavit, there is a fair probability that contraband or evidence of a crime will be found in a particular place. A reviewing court asks only whether the magistrate had a substantial basis for that conclusion. Oath or affirmation is the accountability element - someone swears to the facts and can be prosecuted for lying about them. Particularity is the anti-general-warrant element: the document must name the place and the things, so that the officer executing it is not deciding on the doorstep how far to go.

Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 41 shows what those abstractions look like as paperwork. A judge must find probable cause before issuing. The warrant may reach evidence of a crime; contraband, fruits of crime, or other items illegally possessed; property used in committing a crime; or a person to be arrested or unlawfully restrained. It must identify what is to be searched and anything to be seized, command execution within a specified time no longer than fourteen days, and command daytime execution unless the judge finds good cause otherwise. The executing officer notes the time, prepares a verified inventory, leaves a copy and a receipt, and returns the warrant to the judge. Applications may be made by telephone or other reliable electronic means, which is part of why Riley v. California could tell officers to get a warrant without treating that as a serious obstacle.

Warrants also mark a spatial boundary. Payton v. New York (1980) held that police may not enter a home without a warrant and without consent to make a routine felony arrest, because the Amendment draws a firm line at the entrance to the house that, absent exigent circumstances, may not be crossed.

collegeVersion.heading: The recognized exceptions
collegeVersion.body:
Consent. If a person voluntarily agrees, no warrant and no cause are needed. Schneckloth v. Bustamonte (1973) held that voluntariness is judged from the totality of the circumstances, and that although knowledge of the right to refuse is a factor, the government need not prove the person knew he could say no.

Exigent circumstances. When waiting would defeat the purpose - imminent destruction of evidence, an emergency, an escaping suspect - officers may act without a warrant. Kentucky v. King (2011) added the limit that matters: the exception is available so long as police did not create the exigency by engaging or threatening to engage in conduct that itself violates the Fourth Amendment.

Search incident to lawful arrest. Chimel v. California (1969) confined it to the arrestee's person and the area within his immediate control - the space from which he might grab a weapon or destroy evidence - and required a warrant for other rooms and closed compartments. Arizona v. Gant (2009) applied that logic to cars: officers may search the passenger compartment incident to a recent occupant's arrest only if the arrestee might actually access the vehicle at the time of the search, or if it is reasonable to believe the vehicle contains evidence of the offense of arrest. Gant himself was handcuffed in a patrol car, arrested for driving on a suspended license, so neither branch fit. Riley v. California (2014) drew the line for phones: digital data cannot be used as a weapon and cannot injure anyone, so the Chimel rationales do not reach it, and police generally may not search a phone's contents incident to arrest. The Court's instruction was three words - get a warrant - though exigency remains available in a particular case.

The automobile exception. Carroll v. United States (1925) held that a vehicle may be searched on probable cause that it carries contraband, independent of any right to arrest the driver, reasoning from early customs statutes that treated goods in transit differently from goods concealed in a dwelling. Its rationale is mobility, not a lower status for drivers.

Plain view. Horton v. California (1990) held that inadvertent discovery is not required, then restated what is: the officer must have arrived lawfully at the vantage point, the object's incriminating character must be immediately apparent, and the officer must have a lawful right of access to the object itself.

Stop and frisk. Terry v. Ohio (1968) recognized a brief, lesser intrusion on less than probable cause. Chief Justice Warren's opinion conceded both halves that the state had denied - restraining someone's freedom to walk away is a seizure, and running hands over the outside of clothing is a search - and then held both can be justified when the officer points to specific and articulable facts, together with rational inferences from them, rather than an inchoate and unparticularized suspicion or hunch. The frisk itself is limited to weapons, and only where a reasonably prudent officer would believe safety was at risk. Later cases attached the label reasonable suspicion; the Terry majority never used it.

collegeVersion.heading: Remedy, and the floor states may raise
collegeVersion.body:
A violated right needs a consequence. The main one here is exclusion: evidence obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment is generally kept out of the prosecution's case, and Mapp v. Ohio (1961) made that rule binding on the states. The mechanism is procedural - Rule 41(h) routes a federal defendant to Rule 12 to move to suppress in the trial court - but the stakes are the case.

Exclusion is not automatic. United States v. Leon (1984) held that when officers rely in objectively reasonable good faith on a warrant issued by a detached and neutral magistrate, evidence stays in even if the warrant is later found invalid, because suppressing it would deter nothing. Leon kept limits: the magistrate cannot be a rubber stamp, and an affidavit the affiant knew was false, or recklessly disregarded the truth of, is still open to attack. The rule's longer history and its other exceptions belong to this curriculum's constitutional-protections lesson.

One caution should follow every Fourth Amendment analysis: everything above states a federal floor. As the Court put it in Oregon v. Hass (1975), a state is free as a matter of its own law to impose greater restrictions on police activity than federal constitutional standards require - it simply may not call those restrictions federal constitutional law. Several state supreme courts read their own search-and-seizure provisions more protectively than the Fourth Amendment, so the same conduct can be lawful in a federal prosecution and unlawful under a state constitution. This lesson is educational material about United States law. It is not legal advice, and it does not describe the law of any particular state.

vocabulary.definition: Government conduct that either physically intrudes on a person, house, paper, or effect to obtain information, or that invades an expectation of privacy society is prepared to recognize as reasonable.
A restraint on liberty accomplished either by physical force applied with intent to restrain, or by a show of authority to which the individual submits.

Enough sworn information, judged on the totality of the circumstances, to support a fair probability that contraband or evidence of a crime will be found in a stated place, or that a stated person committed an offense.

The constitutional command that a warrant name the specific place to be entered and the specific persons or things to be taken, which is what distinguishes it from the general warrants the Amendment was written against.
A situation urgent enough - imminent destruction of evidence, an emergency, a fleeing suspect - that acting without judicial authorization first is objectively reasonable.
The authority, arising from a valid custodial arrest, to examine the arrested person and the area from which that person could reach a weapon or destroy evidence.
A rule permitting warrantless seizure of an item whose incriminating character is immediately apparent, when the officer both reached the vantage point lawfully and has lawful access to the item.
A limited pat-down of outer clothing for weapons, permitted during a brief investigative stop when specific articulable facts support a belief that the person is armed and dangerous.
The judicially created remedy that generally bars the prosecution from using, in its case in chief, evidence obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment.
The doctrine allowing evidence to be admitted when officers relied in objectively reasonable fashion on a warrant issued by a neutral magistrate that later proves defective.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Think of the Fourth Amendment as a rule about doors rather than a rule about police. The government can knock and ask. It can look at whatever is already sitting out in the open. But before it opens a door you have shut - a house, a bag, a phone, a car trunk - it usually has to convince a judge that there is a real reason to think something specific is behind that particular door. The judge writes down which door and what the government is looking for. That written note is a warrant. There is a short list of situations where the government does not have to stop and ask a judge first: you said yes; someone is in danger or evidence is about to be destroyed; the thing is already in plain sight; or an officer has just arrested someone and is checking the space right around them for a weapon. The list is short on purpose, and courts keep arguing about its edges, because every new device creates a new kind of door.
eli10.analogy: A warrant works like a hall pass with the destination and the errand written on it. The office does not hand one out because a teacher has a feeling; the teacher has to say what is going on and where. And the pass only covers the trip it names - a pass to the library is not permission to wander through the gym.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks in three places. A hall pass is issued by the same institution that wants the trip; a warrant is deliberately issued by a judge who is not on the investigating team. A student without a pass is simply sent back; evidence gathered without a valid warrant may be excluded from a trial entirely. And there is no hall-pass equivalent of consent or exigency - a school does not have a rule saying the pass is unnecessary if the building is on fire, but Fourth Amendment law has exactly that kind of rule, and most real disputes are about those exceptions rather than about warrants.

workedExample: An officer sees a parked car with a broken taillight and pulls it over. She walks up and asks the driver where he is headed - no justification needed yet, because a question is not a seizure, though the traffic stop itself already is one. Through the open window she sees a bag of pills on the passenger seat, labels facing up. Run the sequence. Looking through a window from a place she is lawfully standing is not a search, since the contents were knowingly exposed. Seizing the bag is a plain-view seizure under Horton if its incriminating character is immediately apparent and she has lawful access to it. If those pills give probable cause to believe the car holds more contraband, Carroll lets her search the vehicle on that cause without a warrant. Suppose she instead arrests the driver, handcuffs him in the patrol car, and then wants to search the passenger compartment. Gant blocks the officer-safety branch, because he cannot reach anything - but the evidence branch may still apply if it is reasonable to believe the car contains evidence of the drug offense he was arrested for. Now she picks up his phone and starts scrolling. Riley stops her. The phone can be secured; its data cannot hurt anyone; absent consent or a genuine exigency, she needs a warrant naming the phone and describing what she is looking for.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing the Fourth Amendment requires a warrant for every search.
commonMistakes.correction: The text forbids unreasonable searches and specifies what a warrant must contain; it never states a universal warrant requirement. Courts presume warrantless searches unreasonable, but consent, exigency, search incident to arrest, the automobile exception, plain view, and Terry stops are all established exceptions, and most real encounters are resolved under one of them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating an officer's command to stop as the moment a fleeing person is seized.
commonMistakes.correction: California v. Hodari D. holds that a show of authority becomes a seizure only when the person submits to it. Anything discarded during flight before submission is not the fruit of a seizure. Physical force is different: Torres v. Madrid holds that force applied with intent to restrain seizes a person even if he keeps going.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming consent is invalid unless the officer first advised the person of the right to refuse.
commonMistakes.correction: Schneckloth v. Bustamonte requires voluntariness judged on the totality of the circumstances. Knowledge of the right to refuse is one factor a court weighs, but the government does not have to prove the person knew he could decline.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading a lawful arrest as authority to search everything the arrestee had with him, including a phone.
commonMistakes.correction: Chimel limits the search to the person and the area within immediate control, Gant limits vehicle searches to reachability or evidence of the offense of arrest, and Riley v. California holds that police generally may not search a phone's digital contents incident to arrest at all - the answer there is a warrant.

commonMistakes.mistake: Concluding that if federal doctrine permits a search, the search is lawful anywhere in the country.
commonMistakes.correction: Federal constitutional doctrine sets a floor, not a ceiling. Oregon v. Hass states that a state may impose greater restrictions on police as a matter of its own law, and several state supreme courts read their own constitutions more protectively than the Fourth Amendment.

compareContrast.distinction: Katz asks whether the government invaded an expectation of privacy society recognizes as reasonable, which can happen with no physical contact at all. Jones asks whether the government physically intruded on a person, house, paper, or effect to gather information. Jones held the privacy test was added to the trespass test, not substituted for it, so either route can establish a search.

Probable cause supports a fair probability that evidence is in a place or that a person committed a crime, and it is what a warrant and a full arrest require. Terry permits a brief stop and a weapons pat-down on less - specific articulable facts and rational inferences from them - because the intrusion is briefer and narrower. A hunch satisfies neither.

Carroll rests on probable cause that the vehicle contains contraband and lets officers search wherever that contraband could be, whether or not anyone is arrested. Gant rests on a custodial arrest and reaches the passenger compartment only if the arrestee can access it or the vehicle plausibly holds evidence of the offense of arrest. The same car search can fail under one and succeed under the other.

Under Hodari D., a show of authority seizes no one until the person submits, so a suspect who keeps running is not yet seized. Under Torres v. Madrid, physical force applied with intent to restrain seizes the person the moment it lands, even if he escapes. Timing, not degree, is what the two rules divide.

keyTakeaway: Work Fourth Amendment problems in sequence - was there a search or seizure, was there a valid warrant, does an exception apply - and remember that the exceptions, not the warrant requirement, decide most cases. This is educational material about United States law, not legal advice, and state constitutions may protect more.

questionBank.prompt: The two-part test asking whether a person exhibited an actual expectation of privacy and whether society is prepared to recognize that expectation as reasonable comes from which part of Katz v. United States?
options: The syllabus prepared by the Reporter of Decisions
Justice Harlan's concurring opinion
Justice Stewart's majority opinion
Justice Black's dissenting opinion
questionBank.explanation: Justice Stewart's majority opinion said the Fourth Amendment protects people rather than places and that its reach cannot turn on physical intrusion, but it never stated the two-part formulation. Justice Harlan, concurring, described the twofold requirement of a subjective expectation of privacy plus one society is prepared to recognize as reasonable, and later cases adopted his phrasing. Justice Black dissented and rejected the Court's reading entirely. A syllabus is not part of the opinion and states no new test.
questionBank.skill: Attributing a legal test to the opinion that actually states it

questionBank.prompt: An officer shouts 'Stop, police!' at a man who keeps running and throws a package into a yard before being tackled a block later. Under California v. Hodari D., when was the man seized?
options: When the officer shouted, because that was a show of authority
When he threw the package, because abandoning property signals submission
When he was tackled, because a show of authority seizes no one until the person submits
He was never seized, because he initially tried to escape
questionBank.explanation: Hodari D. holds that a seizure requires either the application of physical force or, absent force, submission to a show of authority. The shout alone was a show of authority the suspect did not obey, so no seizure occurred then, and discarding property is not submission. The tackle applied physical force, and that is when the seizure occurred - which is why the discarded drugs were not the fruit of a seizure. Fleeing does not immunize a person from later being seized.
questionBank.skill: Applying the submission requirement to identify the moment of seizure

questionBank.prompt: Police lawfully arrest a driver for a traffic offense, handcuff him, and secure him in a patrol car. They then open his smartphone and read his messages without a warrant. What does Riley v. California say about that search?
options: Police generally need a warrant to search the digital contents of a phone, even after a lawful arrest
The search is valid because a phone found on an arrestee is within the area of immediate control
The search is valid because a lawful custodial arrest justifies examining everything in the arrestee's possession
The search is valid only if the phone was unlocked when officers took it
questionBank.explanation: Riley held that police generally may not search digital information on a cell phone seized from an arrested person without a warrant, reasoning that data cannot be used as a weapon and that officers can secure the device against destruction of evidence. The Chimel immediate-control rationale therefore does not extend to the phone's contents, and the arrest alone does not authorize the search regardless of whether the device was locked. The Court did note that exigent circumstances could still justify a warrantless search in a particular case.
questionBank.skill: Applying the limits of search incident to arrest to digital devices

questionBank.prompt: Officers develop probable cause to believe a parked pickup truck contains stolen electronics, but they arrest no one and get no warrant before searching it. Which doctrine, if any, best supports the search, and why does the other candidate fail?
options: Plain view, because probable cause makes an item's incriminating character immediately apparent
Search incident to arrest, because probable cause is functionally equivalent to an arrest
Exigent circumstances, because any vehicle can theoretically be driven away
The automobile exception, because Carroll permits a vehicle search on probable cause independent of any right to arrest, while Gant's rule requires a custodial arrest that never happened here
questionBank.explanation: Carroll v. United States held that the search of a movable vehicle for contraband does not depend on the right to arrest the driver and is lawful where the searching officer has probable cause. Gant's rule is expressly tied to a recent occupant's arrest, and no one was arrested. Plain view requires that an item's incriminating character be immediately apparent to an officer already lawfully positioned, not merely that probable cause exists as to the vehicle. Labeling every car an exigency would swallow the automobile exception's own probable-cause requirement.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing the automobile exception from search incident to arrest and plain view

questionBank.prompt: Under Illinois v. Gates, how should a magistrate decide whether an affidavit establishes probable cause for a search warrant?
options: By requiring separate proof of the informant's veracity and basis of knowledge under a rigid two-pronged test
By determining beyond a reasonable doubt that evidence is present in the place described
By making a practical, common-sense decision, on the totality of the circumstances, whether there is a fair probability that contraband or evidence of a crime will be found in a particular place
By deferring to the officer's sworn conclusion that probable cause exists
questionBank.explanation: Gates abandoned the rigid Aguilar-Spinelli two-pronged test and replaced it with a totality-of-the-circumstances approach, describing the magistrate's task as a practical, common-sense fair-probability judgment, with a reviewing court asking only whether there was a substantial basis for the conclusion. Beyond a reasonable doubt is the trial standard for guilt, not a warrant standard. Deference to a bare officer conclusion is what Leon later described as rubber-stamping, which forfeits the magistrate's neutral role.
questionBank.skill: Stating the operative probable-cause standard for warrant issuance

provenance.rightsStatus: Public-domain primary authority only - U.S. Supreme Court opinions, the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, and the constitutional text. No copyrighted prose adapted; short quoted phrases are legal terms of art attributed to the deciding case.
provenance.transformation: Every case was read in its official U.S. Reports bound-volume PDF from govinfo, or in the supremecourt.gov slip opinion where no bound volume is published, and the text was extracted locally to verify holdings, dates, authorship, and quoted language. Rule 41 was read in the current consolidated Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure PDF. The lesson organizes those holdings into an original three-step analytical sequence written for this curriculum; no source's structure or wording was followed.
